section.title: The Table of Nations
section.sectionRationale: This chapter is a single, deliberate document: the account of Noah's sons and the seventy peoples that came from them. It maps the whole known world back to one family, setting the stage for Babel and for God's choice of one line, Shem, through which all these nations will be blessed.
section.thesis: From Noah's three sons the whole earth is repopulated, so that every nation on the map is one family under God, and the story is quietly narrowing toward the line of Shem.
section.frameNote: Four movements framed by the heading and closing formula: the introduction; the sons of Japheth; the sons of Ham, including Nimrod; and the sons of Shem, the covenant line.

verses.text: This is the account of Noah’s sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, who also had sons after the flood.
The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.
The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.
And the sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, the Kittites, and the Rodanites.
From these, the maritime peoples separated into their territories, according to their languages, by clans within their nations.
The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.
The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. And the sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.
Cush was the father of Nimrod, who began to be a {{gibbor|mighty one}} on the earth.
He was a mighty hunter before the LORD; so it is said, “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD.”
His kingdom began in Babylon, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.
From that land he went forth into Assyria, where he built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah,
and Resen, which is between Nineveh and the great city of Calah.
Mizraim was the father of the Ludites, the Anamites, the Lehabites, the Naphtuhites,
the Pathrusites, the Casluhites (from whom the Philistines came), and the Caphtorites.
And Canaan was the father of Sidon his firstborn, and of the Hittites,
the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites,
the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites,
the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. Later the Canaanite clans were scattered,
and the borders of Canaan extended from Sidon toward Gerar as far as Gaza, and then toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.
These are the sons of Ham according to their clans, languages, lands, and nations.
And sons were also born to Shem, the older brother of Japheth; Shem was the forefather of all the sons of {{eber|Eber}}.
The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram.
The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.
Arphaxad was the father of Shelah, and Shelah was the father of Eber.
Two sons were born to Eber: One was named {{peleg|Peleg}}, because in his days the earth was divided, and his brother was named Joktan.
And Joktan was the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,
Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah,
Obal, Abimael, Sheba,
Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were sons of Joktan.
Their territory extended from Mesha to Sephar, in the eastern hill country.
These are the sons of Shem, according to their clans, languages, lands, and nations.
All these are the clans of Noah’s sons, according to their generations and nations. From these the {{goy|nations}} of the earth spread out after the flood.

gibbor.gloss: A mighty man, warrior, or hero. Nimrod is the first person described this way after the flood, a builder of cities and empires including Babylon. The word can be admiring or ominous, and here it hints at the rise of proud human power that reaches its peak at Babel in the next chapter.

eber.gloss: The ancestor from whose name the word Hebrew is generally derived. By singling out Shem as the forefather of the sons of Eber, the writer flags the family line that leads to Abram the Hebrew and, through him, to Israel and Christ.

peleg.gloss: The name Peleg means division, and it is explained by the note that in his days the earth was divided. This likely points to the scattering at Babel, so the genealogy already carries a trace of the judgment about to be narrated.

goy.gloss: A nation or people, plural goyim. This is the word that will echo through the whole Bible for the nations, or Gentiles. Here every goy on the map is traced to one family, so the later promise that all nations will be blessed through Abram gathers up this very list.

basic.context: After the flood, the world had to be repopulated, and this chapter is like a family map showing where all the nations came from. It traces seventy peoples back to Noah's three sons: Japheth, Ham, and Shem. The big question it answers is simple: where did all the different nations come from?
basic.hermeneutics: The key question is why the Bible gives us a long list of names and places. It is not just a record; it is making a point, that every nation on earth is one family under God. It also slows down over Shem's line, quietly steering us toward the family God will choose.
basic.originalLanguages: Nimrod is called a mighty one, a word that can mean hero or can hint at proud, empire-building power, and his kingdom starts at Babylon. Shem is called the father of the sons of Eber, the name behind the word Hebrew. And one grandson is named Peleg, meaning division, because the earth was split in his days.
basic.typology: This map of all nations sets up a promise: through one man from Shem's line, God will bless every family listed here. The scattered nations of Genesis 10 are gathered again at Pentecost, when people from many nations hear the gospel in their own tongue, and finally in Revelation, where every nation stands before the throne.
basic.christ: The chapter narrows down to Shem, and Shem's line runs to Abraham and then to Jesus. Jesus is the promised descendant through whom the blessing reaches out to every nation on this list, undoing the scattering and gathering a people from all peoples.
basic.god: God is Lord of all the nations, not just one. He is the God who fills the earth with people just as He commanded, and He rules over Babylon and Nineveh and every clan on the map. He is patiently working out a plan to bless them all.
basic.crossReferences: Paul says God made every nation from one man and set their times and places. At Pentecost the scattered languages are reunited in the gospel. And Revelation shows a countless crowd from every nation gathered before the Lamb.
basic.oneStory: This is the world God so loved: seventy nations spread across the earth, all one family, all wandering from Him. The Bible zooms in on Shem's line because that is where the rescuer will come, the one who will bless every nation on this map and gather the scattered peoples home.

context.literary:
Genesis 10 opens with the heading 'This is the account of Noah's sons,' verse 1, the fourth of the 'account' headings that structure Genesis, after Genesis 2:4, 5:1 and 6:9. The next, 'This is the account of Shem,' follows at Genesis 11:10. Inside, the chapter moves in three blocks, Japheth, verses 2 to 5, Ham, verses 6 to 20, and Shem, verses 21 to 31, each closed by a near identical refrain about clans, languages, lands and nations, verses 5, 20 and 31. Verse 32 sums up the whole.

The heading names the sons in birth order, Shem, Ham and Japheth, but the body reverses it and treats Shem last. This is a habit of Genesis: the line that the story will not follow is recorded first and set aside, and the chosen line comes last and is carried forward. Cain's line comes before Seth's, Ishmael's account, Genesis 25:12, before Isaac's, Genesis 25:19, and Esau's, Genesis 36:1, before Jacob's, Genesis 37:2. By listing Shem last, the chapter hands him on to chapter 11.

This is a segmented genealogy, spreading out sideways to show how peoples relate, unlike the straight line genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11:10-26, which run down one line to a single person. Counting every named descendant gives seventy: fourteen from Japheth, thirty from Ham and twenty six from Shem. Seventy is also the number of Jacob's household that went down to Egypt, Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5, so Israel appears in miniature as a counterpart to the nations.

The list is interrupted twice by short narratives: the notice about Nimrod, verses 8 to 12, and the naming of Peleg, verse 25. Both point ahead to Babel. The chapter describes the result of the dispersion, peoples with their own languages, before Genesis 11:1-9 tells how it came about. The order is thematic rather than strictly chronological.
context.historical:
The table maps the world as Israel knew it, arranged roughly by geography. Japheth's line stretches north and west, toward Anatolia, the Aegean and the coasts and islands. Javan is the Hebrew name for the Greeks; Daniel 8:21 speaks of 'the king of Greece,' where the Hebrew is Javan. Madai is Media, Daniel 5:28. The Kittites are associated with Cyprus, which is how the BSB renders the name in Isaiah 23:1 and Jeremiah 2:10. Tarshish was a distant port, the place Jonah tried to flee to, Jonah 1:3.

Ham's line runs south and southwest, into Africa, Arabia and Canaan. Mizraim is the ordinary Hebrew word for Egypt. Cush lies south of Egypt, along the upper Nile, and Put is commonly placed in Libya. Canaan is the land Israel would inherit, and verse 19 traces its borders from Sidon to Gaza and to the cities of the plain, Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, whose fate Genesis 19 will tell.

Shem's line lies to the east: Elam, Asshur or Assyria, Aram and the Arabian peoples of Joktan. Uz, verse 23, is the homeland of Job, Job 1:1. Ophir, verse 29, was known in Israel as the source of Solomon's gold, 1 Kings 9:28, and Sheba sent its queen to test Solomon, 1 Kings 10:1.

The names are a mix of individuals, peoples and places. Some are clearly peoples, the Jebusites, Amorites and Hivites. Some are cities, Sidon and the towns of Nimrod. Some names occur in more than one line: Havilah and Sheba appear under Ham, verse 7, and under Shem, verses 28 and 29, and Sheba and Dedan appear again among Abraham's descendants by Keturah, Genesis 25:3. 'Father of' in a list like this can express descent, political connection or geographical association. The table is a theological map as well as a family record.

Nimrod's cities in verses 10 to 12 name the heartlands of the two great Mesopotamian empires. Babylon, Erech and Accad lay in Shinar, southern Mesopotamia. Nineveh and Calah lay in Assyria. The ruins of Calah are still known today as Nimrud, after the figure of this chapter.
context.canonical:
The table sets the stage for the whole biblical story of the nations. Deuteronomy 32:8 looks back on it: 'When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance, when He divided the sons of man, He set the boundaries of the peoples.' Paul says the same at Athens: 'From one man He made every nation of men ... and He determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands,' Acts 17:26.

The prophets name the peoples of this chapter as they speak of God's rule over all nations. Ezekiel 38 gathers Magog, Meshech, Tubal, Gomer and Togarmah, all from Japheth's line, and Sheba, Dedan and Tarshish. Micah 5:6 calls Assyria 'the land of Nimrod.' Isaiah looks forward to Egypt and Assyria joining Israel in worship: 'Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance,' Isaiah 19:24-25. Isaiah 66:19 sends messengers 'to Tarshish, Put, and the archers of Lud; to Tubal, Javan, and the islands far away' to declare God's glory among the nations. Psalm 87:4 imagines Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush being counted as those born in Zion. Zephaniah 3:9-10 sees worshippers coming 'from beyond the rivers of Cush.'

The New Testament picks up the thread. At Pentecost the crowd includes 'Medes, and Elamites; residents of Mesopotamia,' along with Egypt, Libya, Cretans and Arabs, Acts 2:9-11, a list that reads like a new table of nations hearing the gospel in their own languages. One of the first people from beyond Israel to believe in Acts is an official from Ethiopia, the land of Cush, Acts 8:27. Luke's mission of the seventy two, Luke 10:1, where some manuscripts read seventy, may echo the number of the nations here. And Revelation's vision of a multitude 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue,' Revelation 7:9, uses the same fourfold pattern as the refrains of Genesis 10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to know that they belonged to one human family. Before Israel appears, the whole world is set out as the descendants of Noah, all under the blessing to be fruitful and fill the earth, all within the covenant God made in Genesis 9. The nations around Israel, friends and enemies alike, are Israel's relatives.

He wanted Israel to locate itself on this map. The line of Shem through Eber leads to the Hebrews. The Canaanites, whose land Israel would receive, are placed under Ham, and their borders are drawn in verse 19. Egypt, where Israel was enslaved, and Babylon and Assyria, which would later carry Israel into exile, are all named here. Nothing in Israel's later history involves a people God did not know from the beginning.

He also wanted Israel to see where history was heading. The chapter narrows. Shem is saved for last, Eber is singled out, and Peleg's name is explained. The reader is being prepared for the line that runs to Abram in Genesis 11:10-26. Yet the chapter does not treat the other nations as irrelevant. They are the 'families of the earth' who will be blessed through Abram, Genesis 12:3. Israel's calling would be for the sake of these seventy nations.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Genesis 10 is descriptive, an account of how the earth was peopled after the flood. It contains no commands. Its lasting truths are theological: all people share a common origin, all nations are under God's rule, and God's purposes involve every nation on the map.

That has practical consequences. The chapter gives no ground for treating any ethnic group as less than fully human or outside God's care, and it gives no ground for a ranking of peoples by their ancestor. Ham's line includes Egypt and Canaan, but also Cush and Sheba, whose people are later found worshipping God. The chapter also warns against reading its divisions as permanent. The nations divided by language will be gathered by the gospel.

What carries forward is a vision. The church is called to 'make disciples of all nations,' Matthew 28:19, and Genesis 10 shows who those nations are: a single family, scattered, loved and sought.

debates.question: How should we read the ordering of the chapter, with Japheth first and Shem last?

views.label: A narrowing focus
views.case: Genesis regularly lists the lines it will not follow first, then lingers on the chosen line. Here Shem comes last, is introduced specially in verse 21 as 'the forefather of all the sons of Eber,' and leads straight into his own account in Genesis 11:10. The order marks him as the line the story will follow.

views.label: A geographic sweep
views.case: Others read the order mainly as a movement across the known world, from the distant northern and coastal peoples, to the southern peoples of Africa and Canaan, and finally to the eastern peoples near Mesopotamia. On this view the order is a map rather than a ranking.

debates.bearing: Both are probably true. The chapter is organised geographically, but its placement of Shem last follows the pattern of Genesis and sets up the call of Abram. A table of nations is also a signpost to the story of redemption.

debates.question: Was Nimrod a hero or a tyrant?

views.label: A mighty hunter in God's sight
views.case: The phrase 'before the LORD' often means 'in the sight of' or 'with the favour of' the LORD. The proverb 'Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD' could be a compliment, as though his skill was renowned. Hunting dangerous beasts was a royal activity in the ancient world, a way kings displayed their power to protect.

views.label: A defiant empire builder
views.case: The BSB footnote allows 'in defiance of' the LORD. The word 'mighty one' recalls 'the mighty men of old' before the flood, Genesis 6:4. Nimrod's kingdom begins at Babylon in Shinar, the very place where humanity will build its tower, Genesis 11:2. And his cities include Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. Many read him as the prototype of the proud, violent ruler who builds his own kingdom.

debates.bearing: The text is restrained, but the context leans toward the second reading. Nimrod's kingdom is the setting for Babel, and the empires he founded became Israel's great oppressors. Even so, he is placed 'before the LORD,' under His eye, and God remains Lord of every empire.

debates.question: What was 'divided' in the days of Peleg?

views.label: The dispersion at Babel
views.case: The most common view links verse 25 to Genesis 11:1-9. Peleg means division, and the division of humanity by language and land at Babel would be the most significant division of the age. On this reading, Peleg's naming places Babel within the genealogy.

views.label: A division of land or peoples
views.case: The noun peleg is used elsewhere for a channel or stream, Psalm 1:3 and 46:4. Some suggest the verse refers to the division of land by irrigation channels, or to a political division. Others note that the split in Eber's own family, between Peleg and Joktan, is itself a division, since one line goes to Abram and the other to the Arabian peoples.

debates.bearing: The link to Babel fits the chapter's refrain about languages and its placement just before Genesis 11. The text does not say more, and the other readings remain possible. Whatever the division, it is recorded as part of God's ordering of the nations.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's refrain in verses 5, 20 and 31 uses four words that together describe what a nation is: mishpachot, 'clans'; leshonot, 'languages' or literally 'tongues'; aratsot, 'lands'; and goyim, 'nations.' Kinship, speech, territory and political identity. Revelation 7:9 uses a similar fourfold description, 'every nation and tribe and people and tongue,' and the echo seems deliberate: the categories that describe the scattered peoples of Genesis 10 describe the gathered people of the new creation.

The word mishpachot, 'clans,' in verse 32 is the word God uses in His promise to Abram: 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3. The BSB translates the same Hebrew word as 'clans' in Genesis 10 and 'families' in Genesis 12. In Hebrew the link is plain. The families of Genesis 12:3 are the clans of Genesis 10:32.

Nimrod 'began to be a mighty one,' verse 8. The verb is from chalal, 'to begin,' the verb used at other ominous new starts: humanity beginning to multiply before the flood, Genesis 6:1, and the builders of Babel, 'if they have begun to do this,' Genesis 11:6. 'Mighty one' is gibbor, a word that can mean a warrior, a champion or a hero. It was last used of the 'mighty men of old' of Genesis 6:4. The BSB footnote gives alternatives: 'who established himself as a mighty warrior' or 'who became the first fearless leader.'

'Before the LORD,' lipne YHWH, literally 'to the face of the LORD,' usually means 'in the presence of' or 'in the sight of.' The BSB footnote gives 'in defiance of' as an alternative in verse 9. The same preposition can carry a sense of opposition, 'in the face of,' so the phrase is genuinely ambiguous. Its repetition in a proverb shows Nimrod became a byword, but the text leaves the reader to weigh whether his fame was for good or ill.

'Eber,' verse 21, is the ancestor from whom the word 'Hebrew,' ivri, is usually derived. Abram is the first person in Scripture called 'the Hebrew,' Genesis 14:13. The BSB footnote notes an ambiguity in the same verse: 'Shem, the older brother of Japheth' could also be read 'Shem, whose older brother was Japheth.'

Peleg, verse 25, means 'division,' as the BSB footnote notes, and the verb 'was divided,' niphlegah, is from the same root. The noun peleg also means a channel or stream, as in 'streams of water,' Psalm 1:3. The wordplay binds the name to the event without telling us exactly what that event was.

Finally, the verb 'spread out' in verse 32 is from parad, 'to separate' or 'divide.' It was used of the river that 'branched' into four in Genesis 2:10, and it is used of the maritime peoples who 'separated' in verse 5. Genesis 13:9 and 13:11 use it when Abram and Lot part ways. In Genesis 10 separation is not yet a curse; it is the natural spreading of a blessed humanity, though Babel will show a darker side.

typology.type: The seventy nations of the earth, Genesis 10:32
typology.fulfillment: The table sets out seventy nations descended from Noah, spread across the earth, divided by language and land. The gospel is for exactly this world. At Pentecost people from many of these regions hear the apostles 'declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues,' Acts 2:11, and Jesus sends His disciples to 'make disciples of all nations,' Matthew 28:19. The escalation is that the nations are not simply listed but redeemed: the Lamb purchased 'those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation,' Revelation 5:9. The type falls short only in that the table records a scattering; the gospel records a gathering.

typology.type: The line of Shem through Eber, Genesis 10:21
typology.fulfillment: Shem is singled out as the father of the sons of Eber, the ancestor of the Hebrews, and the genealogy of Genesis 11 carries his line to Abram. Luke traces Jesus through 'Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem,' Luke 3:35-36, and on to Adam, Luke 3:38. The correspondence is a chosen line within the nations. The escalation is that the line exists for the sake of the nations: in Christ, the seed of Abraham, 'All nations will be blessed through you,' Galatians 3:8.

typology.type: Nimrod and his kingdom at Babylon, Genesis 10:8-10
typology.fulfillment: Nimrod is the first empire builder in Scripture, and his kingdom begins at Babylon. From then on Babylon stands for proud human power organised against God: the tower of Genesis 11, the empire that destroyed Jerusalem, and finally 'Babylon the great' of Revelation 17:5, whose fall is announced in Revelation 18:2. This is a type of opposition rather than fulfilment, an anti-kingdom set against the kingdom of God. Christ does not fulfil Nimrod; He overthrows the pattern Nimrod began, establishing a kingdom not built by human might.

typology.type: The scattered sons of Joktan and the undivided family of Noah
typology.fulfillment: The chapter ends by tracing the line of Joktan, which is not the line of promise, before returning to Peleg in Genesis 11. Even the lines that are not followed are named, counted and placed on the map. In Christ the lines that were set aside are drawn in. Isaiah foresaw Egypt and Assyria called God's people and handiwork, Isaiah 19:24-25, and Paul says there is 'no difference between Jew and Greek: The same Lord is Lord of all,' Romans 10:12. The type anticipates the church's calling to every people the table names.

study.christ:
Genesis 10 leads to Christ first through the line it carries forward. The chapter sets Shem last and singles out Eber, and Genesis 11 takes that line to Abram. Luke's genealogy traces Jesus back through Peleg, Eber, Shelah, Cainan, Arphaxad and Shem, Luke 3:35-36, following the Greek Old Testament in including Cainan, as the BSB footnote at Genesis 10:24 notes. Luke's genealogy does not stop at Abraham, as Matthew's does, but runs on to 'Adam, the son of God,' Luke 3:38. The Saviour belongs to Shem's line and to the whole human race.

It leads to Christ through the promise to the nations. The clans of Genesis 10:32 are the families of Genesis 12:3, the same Hebrew word. When God promises Abram that 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' He is promising blessing to this very list. Paul calls that promise the gospel preached in advance: 'The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham,' Galatians 3:8. Christ is the seed of Abraham through whom the blessing reaches the seventy nations.

It leads to Christ through the reversal of the scattering. The chapter's refrain, 'according to their languages,' assumes the confusion of Babel. At Pentecost the Spirit comes on the disciples, and people from Elam, Media, Mesopotamia, Egypt, Libya, Crete and Arabia hear them declaring 'the wonders of God in our own tongues,' Acts 2:11. The languages are not abolished but redeemed. The gospel does not make everyone speak one language; it makes every language a means of praising God.

It leads to Christ through the Great Commission. Jesus sends His disciples to 'make disciples of all nations,' Matthew 28:19, and to be His witnesses 'to the ends of the earth,' Acts 1:8. The Ethiopian official of Acts 8:27, from the land of Cush, and the Greeks, descendants of Javan, to whom Paul preached, are among the first of the table's nations to hear. Jesus says the gospel will be preached 'as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come,' Matthew 24:14.

It leads to Christ through the defeat of Babylon. Nimrod's kingdom begins at Babylon, and Babylon becomes Scripture's name for proud human power. Revelation announces 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!' Revelation 18:2. The kingdom of Christ is the opposite of Nimrod's. Nimrod was a mighty hunter who built cities for his own glory; Christ is the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11, and His people look for the city 'whose architect and builder is God,' Hebrews 11:10.

And it leads to Christ through the final gathering. The Lamb who was slain is worshipped because by His blood He 'purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation,' Revelation 5:9. The table of nations becomes the choir of heaven.

The chapter itself does not name a Messiah, and it would be forced to find Christ hidden in individual names. The link is structural and thematic: the table defines the world to which the promised seed is sent, and the line through which He comes.
study.god:
Genesis 10 reveals God as the Lord of all nations. Israel is not yet on the map, and yet the whole map belongs to God. He is the one who 'gave the nations their inheritance' and 'set the boundaries of the peoples,' Deuteronomy 32:8. Paul makes the same point: God made every nation from one man and 'determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands,' Acts 17:26. The rise and spread of every people is under His governance.

He is faithful to His word. God told Noah and his sons to 'be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth,' Genesis 9:1, and Genesis 10 shows it happening: 'From these the nations of the earth spread out after the flood,' verse 32. The blessing is working. God's word is not frustrated even by human sin.

He is patient. The chapter includes nations that would become Israel's enemies, Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, the Philistines, the Canaanites. God does not wipe them out. He lets them grow, trade, build and rule. His judgments, when they come, come in His time, as with the Canaanites when their iniquity was complete, Genesis 15:16.

He sees even those the story leaves behind. Joktan's thirteen sons, verses 26 to 29, are named although their line is not followed. The Arabian peoples, the islands of the sea and the distant coasts are all counted. Jonah would learn that God cares for Nineveh, one of Nimrod's cities, 'the great city of Nineveh,' Jonah 4:11. The God of the Bible is not a tribal deity.

He is sovereign over the powerful. Nimrod is a mighty one, but he is 'before the LORD,' in His sight and under His judgment. The empires of Babylon and Assyria began here, and Scripture will show God raising them up and bringing them down.

He is moving history toward a purpose. The chapter lists all nations but lingers over Shem and Eber. God is preparing to call one man for the sake of all. This is the tension the chapter holds: universal concern and particular choice. God chooses one line not to exclude the others but to reach them.

For worship, Genesis 10 enlarges our view of God. Every nation on earth is part of the family He made and is seeking. The church's prayer for the nations, and its missionary labour, are grounded in the God of Genesis 10, who knows every clan, language, land and nation by name, and whose purpose is that 'all the families of the nations will bow down before Him,' Psalm 22:27.

crossReferences.note: When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance and divided the sons of man, He set the boundaries of the peoples. Moses' song looks back on Genesis 10 as God's own act of distributing the nations. The BSB footnote notes a textual variant in the last phrase.

The tower of Babel tells how the languages and lands of Genesis 10 came about. The table gives the result and Babel gives the cause. Nimrod's Babylon in Genesis 10:10 and the plain of Shinar in Genesis 11:2 are the same place.

All the families of the earth will be blessed through Abram. The Hebrew word for families is the same word translated clans in Genesis 10:32, so the promise to Abram is aimed at exactly the peoples listed in the table.

Jacob's household that went down to Egypt numbered seventy. The number matches the seventy names of the table, and Israel appears as a small counterpart to the nations, a people set within the world for its sake.

The land of Assyria is called 'the land of Nimrod.' The prophet assumes the connection in Genesis 10:11 between Nimrod and Assyria, and promises a ruler from Bethlehem, Micah 5:2, who will deliver Israel from Nimrod's heirs.

Isaiah foresees Egypt and Assyria joining Israel as a blessing on the earth: 'Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork.' Mizraim from Ham's line and Asshur from Shem's line, two of Israel's great oppressors, are gathered into God's people.

Paul tells the Athenians that from one man God made every nation and determined their times and boundaries. This is Genesis 10 in a sentence, and Paul uses it to call the nations to seek God, who is not far from each of them.

At Pentecost people from Media, Elam, Mesopotamia, Egypt, Libya, Crete and Arabia hear the apostles in their own languages. The list reads like a new table of nations, and the gift of tongues begins to undo the scattering Genesis 10 records.

An Ethiopian official, from the land the Old Testament calls Cush, hears the gospel and is baptised. Cush is the first son of Ham listed in Genesis 10:6, and a man from that land becomes one of the first from beyond Israel in Acts to believe.

Luke's genealogy traces Jesus through Abraham back to Peleg, Eber, Shelah, Cainan, Arphaxad and Shem, and beyond to Adam. The line singled out in Genesis 10:21-25 leads to Christ, and Luke follows the Greek Old Testament in including Cainan.

A multitude from every nation, tribe, people and tongue stands before the Lamb. The fourfold description echoes the clans, languages, lands and nations of Genesis 10, and shows the scattered family of Noah gathered in worship.

The leaves of the tree of life are for the healing of the nations. The nations of Genesis 10, spread out and divided, are not erased in the new creation but healed, and they walk by the light of the city, Revelation 21:24.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 10 shows the blessing of creation at work. God told the first humans to 'fill the earth,' Genesis 1:28, and He repeated it to Noah, Genesis 9:1. Now, after the flood, the earth is being filled. The chapter answers the question the flood raised, whether humanity would continue, with a map of seventy nations spreading across the world. God's purpose for a filled and fruitful earth has not been abandoned.

But the map is also a record of a world still under the fall. The refrain 'according to their languages' points to the confusion at Babel, where humanity tried to make a name for itself and was scattered. Nimrod's kingdom begins at Babylon, and proud empires begin their long history. The nations are one family, but a divided and wandering one.

The chapter sets up what follows by narrowing. Shem is placed last, Eber singled out, Peleg named. Genesis 11 follows that line to Abram, and Genesis 12 gives him the promise: 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.' From there the story follows one family, Israel, but it never forgets the other sixty nine. Israel's psalms and prophets keep looking back to the table and forward to the day when the nations stream to Zion, Isaiah 2:2-3.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, the son of Shem and the son of Adam, through whom the blessing to Abraham comes to the nations. At Pentecost the scattered languages hear one gospel. The apostles carry it to Cush, to Javan and to the ends of the earth.

And the story ends where Genesis 10 points. John sees a multitude 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue' before the Lamb, Revelation 7:9. The nations are still nations, with their languages and identities, but they are no longer scattered and estranged. They walk by the light of the city of God, Revelation 21:24, and the leaves of the tree of life are 'for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:2. The family of Noah, divided at Babel, is finally gathered as one people of God.

quiz.q: What is the main point of the Table of Nations?

options.text: Every nation on earth descends from Noah's one family under God.
options.note: The chapter traces all peoples back to a single family and God's rule over them.

options.text: It records the names of Israel's kings.
options.note: There are no kings of Israel here; it lists the descent of the nations.

options.text: It lists the nations mainly to fill space before the next story.
options.note: The list is deliberate and theological, not filler.

options.text: It maps the neighbours and powers Israel would later meet.
options.note: True and useful, but the deeper point is the unity of all nations under God.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter give special attention to Shem's line?

options.text: Because the covenant line to Abraham and Christ runs through Shem.
options.note: Shem is father of the sons of Eber, the line that leads to the Saviour.

options.text: Because Shem had the most children.
options.note: The focus is on the covenant line, not on numbers.

options.text: Because Shem's descendants were the most powerful.
options.note: Nimrod from Ham's line builds the great empires; Shem matters for the promise, not power.

options.text: For no particular reason at all.
options.note: The attention to Shem is deliberate and points to Christ.

quiz.q: Who is Nimrod in this chapter?

options.text: A mighty one whose kingdom began at Babylon in Shinar.
options.note: He is the first great empire-builder, linked to Babylon and Nineveh.

options.text: A faithful worshipper of the LORD.
options.note: The text calls him mighty and a city-builder; it does not commend his faith.

options.text: A son of Shem in the covenant line.
options.note: Nimrod descends from Ham through Cush, not from Shem.

options.text: A hunter and ruler whose cities include Nineveh.
options.note: True, though the striking detail is that his kingdom starts at Babylon.

quiz.q: How are the scattered nations of this chapter finally gathered?

options.text: In Christ, at Pentecost and before the throne, from every nation.
options.note: The gospel reunites the peoples that were scattered.

options.text: Through the empire of Babylon uniting them by force.
options.note: Babylon divides and oppresses; it is not the true gathering.

options.text: Partly through Israel drawing the nations to the temple.
options.note: A real Old Testament hope, but its fulfilment is in Christ and the gospel.

options.text: They are never gathered; they stay divided forever.
options.note: Revelation shows every nation gathered before the Lamb.

quiz.q: What does the name Peleg signal in the genealogy?

options.text: Division, because in his days the earth was divided.
options.note: The name carries a trace of the scattering narrated at Babel.

options.text: Blessing, because his line was especially favoured.
options.note: The name means division, not blessing.

options.text: Mighty one, like Nimrod.
options.note: That title belongs to Nimrod, not Peleg.

options.text: A hint that judgment and scattering are woven into the story.
options.note: This is the right implication, though the name itself specifically means division.

questions: The whole human race is one family here. How does it change the way you see people of other nations to know they are your distant relatives under one God?
God rules over Babylon and Nineveh as surely as over His own people. Where do you need to trust that God is still Lord over powers that look bigger than you?
The chapter quietly narrows to one family so a Saviour can come for all. Where are you tempted to think God only cares about the big and powerful, not the small and chosen?
The nations scattered here are gathered again in Christ. Who in your life feels far off and unreachable, and how might the gospel be for them too?
Nimrod built cities to make himself great. What are you building, and is it for your own name or for God's?

translationNotes.note: The refrain according to their languages assumes the scattering of Babel that follows in chapter eleven; Genesis 10 gives the outcome, chapter eleven gives the cause.

The phrase a mighty hunter before the LORD can be read positively as in the sight of the LORD or negatively as in defiance of the LORD, and Nimrod's link to Babylon inclines many toward the ominous sense.
